extracted.intended_audience: taxpayers, tax professionals, employers and payroll/reporting entities (including digital content creators and gig workers)
extracted.subtask_description: Final Treasury/IRS regulations and explanatory preamble interpreting section 224 of the Internal Revenue Code, providing the criteria for which tips are 'qualified tips', which occupations are on the List of Occupations that Receive Tips, and related reporting and examples. Guidance targets taxpayers, reporting entities, and practitioners determining eligibility for the section 224 deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of Occupations that Receive Tips — Secretary-provided, fixed-date list
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 224(d)(1) requires that qualified tips are cash tips received by an individual in an occupation which customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024, 'as provided by the Secretary.' The List of Occupations that Receive Tips is therefore the comprehensive list provided by the Secretary and is tied to that fixed point in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute contemplates one exhaustive list as of December 31, 2024; the final regulations retain the proposed requirement that only tips received in connection with occupations on that list are eligible for the section 224 deduction. Through the notice-and-comment process interested parties could suggest additions, and the Treasury and IRS revised the proposed list in response to comments, but the final list is the authoritative list for eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupations on the list may include workers without extensive customer interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike the FLSA's 'customarily and regularly receive tips' construct (which contemplates some level of customer interaction and a $30/month threshold), section 224(d)(3) provides that cash tips include tips received through a tip sharing arrangement; accordingly, the List of Occupations that Receive Tips may include occupations that may not have extensive, or any, customer interaction (e.g., dishwashers and cooks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations adopt the Treasury/IRS approach of including occupations that receive tips through tip-sharing arrangements even if they would not be considered 'tipped' under the FLSA; inclusion under section 224 has no bearing on FLSA determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative examples are non-exhaustive
rubrics_metrics.description: The illustrative examples provided under each TTOC (Taxonomy/Taxonomy of Occupations that Receive Tips category) are intended to assist taxpayers but are not an exhaustive list of every occupation that fits under that category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There may be other occupations that fall within a TTOC that are not listed as an illustrative example; taxpayers should interpret TTOC categories consistent with their commonly understood meaning and the explanatory description included with each category (the IRS intends fair and impartial interpretation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxpayer and reporter responsibility to ensure occupation is on the list
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxpayers wishing to claim the deduction and entities responsible for information reporting are primarily responsible for ensuring their occupation is on the List of Occupations that Receive Tips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In most instances the list is sufficiently specific to provide clarity. The IRS intends to interpret occupations on the list consistent with commonly understood meaning, but the obligation to verify falls on taxpayers/reporting entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-driven inclusion standard for adding occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: In evaluating comments and possible additions, the Treasury and IRS consulted data sources (2023 income tax return data, preliminary 2024 data, IRS voluntary tip reporting program data, legislative history and survey data regarding tipped occupations), and examined both SOC Codes and occupations as listed on individual income tax returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agencies will add an occupation as a TTOC only where the underlying data support that the occupation customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024. Examples given: added Floral Designers (TTOC 510), Visual Artists (TTOC 509), and Gas Pump Attendants based on this data review; occupations lacking supportive data (e.g., accountants, chiropractors) were not added.

rubrics_metrics.name: No industry-only basis for inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no statutory authority to include an occupation solely because it is practiced in a particular industry; only occupations that customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024 are included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments requesting whole-industry categories (e.g., entire gaming industry) are assessed on whether each specific occupation meets the tipping criterion based on data, not industry membership alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify and adjust TTOC category names and illustrative examples as needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Category names and illustrative examples may be revised for clarity (e.g., changing 'Eyebrow Threading and Waxing Technicians' to 'Eyebrow and Eyelash Technicians'; adding 'doorman' to Baggage Porters and Bellhops; amending 'Food Servers, Non-restaurant' to 'Food and Beverage Servers, Non-restaurant').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such edits clarify coverage (including indoor and outdoor travel guides, banquet wait staff, app-based delivery persons) while preserving that illustrative examples remain non-exhaustive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of app/platform-based delivery and wording about routes
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations remove the phrase 'over established routes or within an established territory' from the description of 'Goods Delivery People' to clarify that app/platform based delivery persons are covered; illustrative examples focus on the service rather than the method of request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: App-based delivery workers are expressly added as illustrative examples to 'Goods Delivery People' (TTOC 804) and to 'Taxi and Rideshare Drivers and Chauffeurs' (TTOC 802).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified tips must be voluntary, without consequence, not negotiated, and determined by the payor
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 224(d)(2)(A) requires that qualified tips are paid 'voluntarily without any consequence in the event of nonpayment' and not 'the subject of negotiation.' The proposed and final regulations provided that amounts are qualified tips only if they are paid voluntarily and without consequence, are not the subject of negotiation, and are determined by the payor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automatic gratuities, service charges, and mandatory amounts automatically added to a customer's bill by the vendor or establishment are not qualified tips, even if subsequently distributed to employees, unless the customer is expressly provided an option to disregard or modify the amount (including reducing it to zero). The final regulations clarify that the customer's option must allow reducing the tip amount to zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic gratuities/service charges excluded absent customer option to decline
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatic gratuities added to a bill with no explicit option for the customer to decline or adjust are mandatory and therefore not qualified tips; the customer's choice to not patronize the business is not equivalent to an option to decline a gratuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revenue Ruling 2012-18 factors (free from compulsion; customer has unrestricted right to determine amount; not subject of negotiation or dictated by employer policy; customer generally determines who receives payment) are consistent with this rule and inform determinations. No transition rule for 2025 was adopted to treat service charges as tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: POS systems and 'tip slider' guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: POS systems that expressly provide the customer an option to disregard or modify amounts added to a bill are voluntary; the final regulations make clear the customer must be able to reduce the tip amount to zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tip selection methods such as POS tip sliders that go to zero or an 'other' option allowing manual zero entry constitute voluntary tipping practices and are examples in the final regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual suggested tips — when they are voluntary
rubrics_metrics.description: If contract terms merely add a discretionary tip as a 'convenience' subject to customer agreement (and nonpayment would not affect scope or cost of service), the tip may be voluntary. If failure to agree to a tip amount results in a higher price (i.e., nonpayment has consequence), the tip is not 'without consequence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether nonpayment is 'without consequence' depends on facts and circumstances; final regulations include an example where a contractual tip is a qualified tip because nonpayment would not affect scope or cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital content creator payments — tip vs. compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Payments that enable a customer to gain access to content are compensation (not tips); voluntary payments made after the customer has already gained access to content are tips if voluntary and otherwise satisfy requirements for qualified tips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience engagement mechanisms that provide superficial digital rewards (highlighted messages, negligible-value tokens) do not disqualify an otherwise qualified tip. If a hosting platform retains a portion of a payment, the retained portion is not received by the individual content creator and is not a qualified tip for the creator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified tip must be 'received by an individual' — platform-retained portions excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: For the statute, the term 'individual' refers to the person performing the services and receiving tips in connection with those services and does not include an entity that facilitates payment or transmits amounts between customers and service providers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any portion of a user's payment retained by a host platform (not an occupation on the List) is not received by the individual content creator and is not a qualified tip for section 224 purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting requirement — only reported tips are eligible (information returns/Form 4137)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 224(a) allows a deduction only for amounts of qualified tips that are 'included on statements furnished to the individual pursuant to section 6041(d)(3), section 6041A(e)(3), section 6050W(f)(2), or section 6051(a)(18), or reported by the taxpayer on Form 4137 (or successor).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regulations clarify that amounts received as a tip that are not separately reported to an individual on one of those statements or reported on Form 4137 (or successor) are not eligible for the deduction. Issues about providing a mechanism for independent contractors to report unreported tips are beyond the scope of these regulations; the reporting requirement is statutory and serves as an anti-abuse measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managers/supervisors receiving tips via tip-pool — ineligible; direct service tips may be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Under FLSA rules, managers and supervisors are prohibited from receiving tips from a tip pool; the final regulations provide that amounts received by a manager or supervisor through a voluntary or mandatory tip-sharing arrangement such as a tip pool are not qualified tips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, amounts received directly by a supervisor or manager for services they provided in the course of duties performed in an occupation that customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024, are qualified tips if all other requirements for qualified tips are met. The final regulations include two examples demonstrating this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: GITCA/TRDA participants — no automatic occupation safe harbor
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no basis in section 224 to automatically consider participants in a GITCA (Gratuity Income Transition Compensation Agreement) or a Tip Rate Determination Agreement (TRDA) as working in occupations on the List of Occupations that Receive Tips; an occupation not customarily and regularly tipped on or before December 31, 2024, is not eligible even if tipping occurs in specific contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed provision allowing GITCA participants to claim the deduction based on designated tip rates is included in the final regulations. The final regulations also do not add a safe harbor for GITCA/TRDA participants to be treated as in qualifying occupations, nor do they exclude otherwise eligible individuals from the deduction merely for being GITCA participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and clarifications to assist application (POS, contracts, digital creators)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations include multiple examples to illustrate application of the voluntary-tip rule (POS tip sliders, contract tips that are or are not without consequence) and examples clarifying tipping vs compensation for digital content creators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples are intended to clarify fact-specific applications (e.g., when a suggested gratuity in contract qualifies as a tip, when 'super chats' are tips vs compensation). Revenue Ruling 2012-18 is consistent with these rules and may be considered for future updates, but updates to that ruling are outside scope of these final regulations.
